title: Unveiling the Basin-Like Loss Landscape in Large Language Models
claim: Larger models show wide flat low-loss basins in parameter space, outside of which capabilities abruptly collapse, consistently across model families.
layout: 3 panels in a row, one per model, shared legend style
description: Three side-by-side line plots show loss on the y-axis (0 to 1.0) against a perturbation scale alpha on the x-axis, one for each model family: (a) Llama, (b) Qwen, (c) Mistral. Each plot has four colored curves for capability benchmarks: Safety (blue), Math (orange), Basic (green), Coding (red). All curves form a basin shape: loss stays near 0 in a wide central region around alpha = 0, then rises sharply to a plateau at 1.0 on both sides. The basin width differs by model. Qwen's x-range is wider (±0.01) than Llama's and Mistral's (±0.004). Mistral has the narrowest, steepest-walled basin. Safety, shown in blue, has a slightly shifted or elevated floor in some panels. Legends sit at the lower left of each panel, and captions (a), (b), (c) appear below in large serif font. The eye goes to the U-shaped dips.
caption: The most-case loss landscape of different models. Specific benchmarks and visualization details are provided in [ref]. As shown, the loss landscape of LLMs resembles a basin, within which models perform nearly identically and outside of which they lose all capabilities. The raw data are presented in [ref], and the 3D version is shown in [ref].
abstract: We discover the emergence of \textit{basins} in the loss landscape of large language models. As model scale increases, LLMs become progressively more resilient to random perturbations in the parameter space, giving rise to expansive stability regions where models exhibit nearly identical performance, but outside of which their capabilities collapse. We observe that pre-training creates a \textit{basic capability} basin, and subsequent alignment fine-tuning forms \textit{specific capability} basins (e.g., safety, math, coding). Thus, we argue that benign fine-tuning confined to the basin should preserve prior capabilities. Besides, we also analyze the loss landscape for worst-case directions, which is consistently sharp and detrimental. We find that adversarial fine-tuning moves along the nearly worst-case directions, thus rapidly degrading model capabilities. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the basin size bounds the performance degradation of any fine-tuning, including the adversarial ones, while also guaranteeing the model robustness w.r.t. input perturbations, suggesting the benefit of enlarging basins.
